screens.body:
Your functions pass their unit tests. Then you plug them together — and everything breaks. Welcome to integration.

Integration is where the pieces talk: the frontend calls the API, the API queries the database. Integration testing checks those conversations, not the individual pieces.
screens.heading: When pieces meet
screens.keyPoint: Units pass alone; integration tests the conversations.

screens.body:
Example: a user signs up. The frontend sends the data, the API validates it, the database stores it, a welcome email fires. An integration test runs that whole chain with test data.

It uses real collaborators (or close fakes) — a test database, not the production one. Never test against real user data.

options: A test database, never production data
check.question: Integration tests should use…

screens.heading: Integration testing, concretely
screens.keyPoint: Test the chain with test data — never production.

screens.body:
System testing zooms all the way out: the complete app, in an environment that looks like production. Does the deployed build actually work?

This is where you catch the "works on my machine" bugs — wrong environment variables, missing files, a database the app can't reach.

options: The whole app in a production-like environment
check.question: System testing runs…

screens.heading: System testing: the whole thing
screens.keyPoint: Test the deployed build, not just your laptop.

screens.body:
Acceptance testing asks a different question: did we build the right thing? The customer — or real users — try the app and confirm it meets their needs.

UAT (user acceptance testing) is the classic form: hand it to actual users before launch and watch what happens. Their confusion is your bug list.

options: Real users trying the app before launch
check.question: UAT is…

screens.heading: Acceptance testing: did we build the right thing?
screens.keyPoint: Real users confirm it meets their needs.

screens.body:
Some collaborators are too risky or expensive to use in tests: payment gateways, SMS services, email providers. So you fake them with sandboxes and test doubles.

Stripe gives you test API keys that behave like the real thing without moving money. Use them. A test that charges a real card is a bug in your test suite.

options: Sandbox/test API keys — never real charges
check.question: For payment testing, use…

screens.heading: Faking the outside world
screens.keyPoint: Sandbox the risky stuff — never charge real cards in tests.

screens.body:
End-to-end tests — a real browser clicking through your real app — are powerful but slow and flaky. A tiny UI change can break dozens of them.

So you write fewer of them, and aim them at critical paths: sign up, post a task, pay. The happy paths that must never break.

options: Critical user paths, in small numbers
check.question: E2E tests should target…

screens.heading: The top of the pyramid is expensive
screens.keyPoint: Few E2E tests, aimed at critical paths.

screens.body:
SwiftGigs is integration-heavy: React app → Supabase → Stripe. Each piece works alone, but the money flows through the chain.

Your beta testers — those 40+ waitlist users — are doing acceptance testing right now. Their feedback is worth more than a hundred unit tests for answering "did we build the right thing?"
screens.heading: Why this matters for you
screens.keyPoint: Your beta testers are your acceptance testers.
